newsitem.title: GERMANY: German budget woes hamper new military role.
newsitem.headline: German budget woes hamper new military role.

text.p: Germany's post-unification drive to play a new military role in the world has cleared all the post-war legal and political hurdles before it, but Bonn's current budget woes now threaten to bog the campaign down.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe, who has slowly given German troops a higher profile in peacekeeping missions abroad, said on Friday the military was in deep financial difficulties due to Bonn's efforts to meet Maastricht's tight spending limits.
Both government and opposition defence experts warned that the cuts threatened the effectiveness of an army falling behind in maintaining basic equipment like trucks and helicopters.

Ruehe said he still planned to contribute troops for the follow-on to the NATO-led peace Implementation Force (IFOR) in Bosnia, but the funds for them -- up to 400 million marks ($265 million) -- would have to be squeezed out of his already shrunken budget.
"We're in a very difficult financial situation," he said after yet another emergency budget meeting in Bonn. "We still have difficulty financing important investments.
"We have to save everywhere -- there's no way around it."

Ruehe, who has seen his budget shrink by one-quarter in the last five years, said Bonn had made no final decision about its planned purchase of 180 Eurofighter combat aircraft. Last month, it cancelled a missile deal with France.

Since reuniting in 1990, the military has slowly shed its post-war shackles and joined international peacekeeping missions in Cambodia, Somalia and Bosnia. Chancellor Helmut Kohl says Germany must shoulder the same burdens as its allies.

A landmark supreme court decision in 1994 ruled that the military could serve outside the NATO area. Last year, the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) and Greens voted with the government to send German troops to join IFOR to Bosnia.

Those troops still had limits on the types of weapons they could use and the kind of tasks they could carry out. The new mission will be the first to put German soldiers on a par with their NATO allies.
Dietrich Austermann, a parliamentary budget committee member from Kohl's Christian Democratic party (CDU), said there was little chance of more money for defence in the coming years.
"I would be more careful about offering German help around the world before looking into the budget," he said.

"Next year's defence budget is the lowest since 1982," he told German radio. "Nobody can just come along and say we'll buy a new fighter jet or a space-based reconnaissance programme or all kinds of new projects without this having any effect."

Apart from the Eurofighter joint venture with Britain, Italy and Spain, Germany also has plans with France for the seven billion mark Helios 2 spy satellite Paris wants to ensure that Europe is less dependent on U.S. intelligence. Ruehe has said he cannot afford this but Kohl still backs the project.
The Defence Ministry revealed on Thursday that it had up to 800 million marks of unpaid bills to be funded in the 1997 budget.
Adding in extra costs like the Bosnia mission, it said: "An already foreseeable burden on the 1997 budget totalling between 1.5 and two billion marks is not unrealistic."
Ruehe reluctantly agreed last summer to cut his 1997 budget target to 46.5 billion marks from the 48.5 billion he wanted. The 1996 defence budget amounts to 47.1 billion marks.
"We can't keep using the military as a quarry for savings," SPD defence spokesman Walter Kolbow said. "We want to have an effective military but it is being increasingly hollowed out."

According to German press reports, about half the army's tanks and one-fifth of its helicopters are out of order but cannot be repaired due to lack of money. There are funds to overhaul only half the trucks needing routine repairs. ($1=1.5104 Mark)
